what_it_does: Modern processors keep a large, shared last-level cache (LLC) — a fast memory buffer close to the chip that stores recently used data for all programs running on the system. A side-channel attack is one where an attacker infers a victim program's secret data not by breaking encryption directly but by observing a physical side effect, such as timing how long cache accesses take. AMD's Zen processors use a non-inclusive cache design, meaning data in the LLC is not guaranteed to also be in smaller, faster caches — a property previously thought to make LLC-based side-channel attacks impractical because an attacker cannot easily figure out which cache slot holds which address. ZenLeak defeats that assumption by painstakingly reverse-engineering exactly how AMD's hardware maps memory addresses to LLC locations (slices and sets), then constructing eviction sets — carefully chosen groups of memory addresses that, when accessed, reliably push a target address out of the cache — to detect whether the victim's program accessed a specific address. The paper demonstrates the attack end-to-end by recovering a secret encryption key from OpenSSL's AES implementation.
